title: How to Reduce Contact Center Call Volume Using Customer Feedback Analysis
summary: Reduce contact center call volume: use customer feedback to find your top contact drivers, separate avoidable failure demand, and fix the cause upstream.
body_text: Every inbound call has a reason, and most of those reasons are written down somewhere: in the call summary, the follow-up survey, the support ticket that came before the call, the one-star review that came after. Contact center teams under pressure to cut volume usually reach for deflection tactics first, more IVR options or a bigger help center. The faster path is to read the feedback you already have, find the handful of issues driving the most calls, and fix them at the source so the calls never happen. You reduce contact center call volume with customer feedback analysis by finding the top reasons customers contact you, separating the avoidable contacts from the necessary ones, and fixing the upstream cause of the avoidable ones. Thematic does this by unifying calls, tickets, chats, and surveys into one intelligence layer, quantifying the themes driving contact volume, and tying each one back to the raw comments so a team knows exactly what to fix first. The economics are hard to ignore: Gartner puts the cost of a live contact around $8.01 , against roughly $0.10 for self-service. Below is a five-step process, a worked example, and the mistakes that keep teams stuck. The five-step process Capture the reason behind every contact. Unify call summaries, tickets, chats, and post-contact surveys in one place. Quantify the top contact drivers. Rank the recurring themes by volume, sentiment, and cost, not ticket by ticket. Separate failure demand from value demand. Tell the avoidable contacts apart from the necessary ones. Fix the top drivers at the source. Change the product, process, or proactive communication that causes the contact. Deflect what remains and track repeat contacts. Route the rest to self-service that actually resolves, and watch the repeat contact rate. Step 1: Capture the reason behind every contact You cannot reduce what you cannot see. The first step is to bring every signal about why customers are contacting you into one place: call and chat transcripts, support tickets, post-contact survey verbatims, app reviews, and complaints. The common mistake here is analyzing one channel in isolation, usually survey responses, while the blunter language lives in tickets and calls. Thematic unifies these sources into a single intelligence layer so the reason for contact is read across the whole journey, not one survey at a time. Atom Bank unified feedback from seven channels across three product lines, including App Store reviews, Trustpilot, support complaints, and call summaries. Step 2: Quantify the top contact drivers Once the feedback is unified, the goal is to find the small number of themes generating the largest share of contacts. This is where teams that tag tickets by hand fall down: a fixed category list drifts, and manual tagging cannot keep pace with volume. Thematic discovers themes from the feedback itself and ranks them by volume, sentiment , and impact, so a team sees which issues are driving the most contact and how customers feel about each. Pair each theme with a cost figure and the priority becomes obvious. At around $8.01 per live contact, a theme responsible for 10,000 avoidable calls a year is an $80,000 problem, and it is now visible next to the exact comments behind it. Step 3: Separate failure demand from value demand Not every call is a problem to be removed. The useful distinction, coined by systems thinker John Seddon, is between value demand and failure demand . Value demand is a customer contacting you for something you want them to contact you about. Failure demand is demand caused by a failure to do something, or to do something right, for the customer. Failure demand is the volume you can actually eliminate. A customer calling because a status email never arrived, an instruction was unclear, or a fee was a surprise is a call you created upstream. Thematic makes this separation practical by surfacing the themes tied to broken processes and unclear communication, so a team can quantify how much of its volume is avoidable rather than guess. Step 4: Fix the top drivers at the source This is the step that removes calls. For each top failure-demand driver, trace it to its root cause and fix it upstream rather than handling each contact one at a time. Common fixes the feedback will point to: Rewrite a confusing instruction, policy, or error message that generates repeat questions. Add or repair a proactive notification so customers stop calling to ask for a status. Fix the product or process defect behind a recurring complaint. Build or correct the self-service content for an issue customers currently have to call about. Because every Thematic theme links back to the raw comments, the team fixing the issue can read the actual customer language behind it, which makes the root cause concrete instead of a category label. Step 5: Deflect what remains and track repeat contacts After the upstream fixes, route the remaining avoidable contacts to self-service. One caution: deflection only works when the self-service option actually resolves the issue. Gartner found that only 9% of customers report fully resolving their issue through self-service, so deflection that just hides the phone number backfires into repeat contacts and higher effort. Track the repeat contact rate as your control metric. Repeated contact is one of the strongest drivers of customer disloyalty, per the CEB research behind The Effortless Experience, so a falling repeat rate means you are removing effort , not just deflecting it. Thematic keeps this honest by scoring the themes over time, so a driver you thought you fixed shows back up in the data if it did not actually go away. A worked example: Atom Bank Atom Bank, the UK app-based digital bank, ran exactly this play. The team unified feedback from seven channels across three product lines into a single 0 to 100 Customer Goodwill score, then used it to identify the top three reasons customers were contacting the bank. Acting on those drivers, Atom Bank cut calls related to unaccepted mortgage requests by 69%, savings maturities by 43%, and device issues by 40%, alongside a 40% reduction in overall call center volume. Contact center failure demand fell by about 30%. Over the same period, the customer base grew 110%, so the volume reduction came while the bank was adding customers, not shedding them. The calls did not move to another channel. The reasons for them were removed. Common mistakes to avoid Deflecting before diagnosing. Adding Interactive Voice Response (IVR) steps or a chatbot in front of an unfixed problem raises effort and repeat contacts. Find the driver first. Counting contacts instead of costing them. Frequency alone misleads. Rank drivers by volume and cost so you fix the expensive ones, not just the loud ones. Treating every ticket as unique. The point of feedback analysis is to see the pattern across thousands of contacts, then fix the shared root cause once. Trusting a score with no comments behind it. If you cannot read the verbatims that produced a theme, you cannot defend the fix or confirm it worked. Removing value demand. Cutting contacts customers genuinely need damages the relationship. Only failure demand is fair game. The short version: reduce call volume by reading the feedback you already collect, ranking the contact drivers by volume and cost, separating avoidable failure demand from genuine value demand, and fixing the top avoidable drivers upstream. Thematic makes that feedback loop fast and traceable. Start by pulling your last 90 days of contact reasons and asking how many were failures you could have prevented.

title: The Human Hiring Advantage: Why Talent Acquisition Still Requires People
summary: How AI overlooks high-potential candidates, and why human insight is essential to finding them.
body_text: The Human Hiring Advantage: Why Talent Acquisition Still Requires People 7:56 After more than two decades in talent acquisition, I've learned one simple truth: The best hires rarely look perfect on paper. Some of the strongest candidates I've ever placed had unconventional career paths. Others lacked a specific credential, industry background, or keyword that many hiring systems are designed to prioritize. Yet they became top performers because someone took the time to understand their potential, not just their resume. Today, that human element is becoming increasingly rare. Organizations are under pressure to fill positions faster, reduce hiring costs, and do more with fewer resources. As a result, many companies have turned to automated screening tools and AI-driven hiring platforms to manage growing applicant volumes. Technology absolutely has a place in recruiting, but when technology becomes the decision-maker instead of a tool, employers risk missing the exact talent they're trying to find. The Rise of Algorithmic Hiring Today, more than 90% of U.S. employers use hiring algorithms to screen or rank applicants before a recruiter ever reviews their qualifications. Recent research examining more than 4 million job applications found that automated systems increasingly influence who gets considered and who never receives a second look. The goal is understandable. Businesses want efficiency, consistency, and to identify qualified candidates faster. The challenge is that people are not data points. Most hiring algorithms are designed to identify patterns. They look for specific keywords, job titles, years of experience, educational backgrounds, and similarities to candidates who have been hired in the past. What they often struggle to identify is potential. A resume can tell you where someone has worked, but it cannot identify the qualities that often determine long-term success: How they lead through adversity How quickly they learn How they fit within a company culture How they contribute to a growing team What the Research Reveals Researchers found that 4% of applicants who applied to ten different jobs were rejected from every opportunity, at a rate higher than chance would predict. In many cases, similar algorithms were making similar decisions across multiple employers. This means a candidate may hear "no" repeatedly, not because they lack capability, but because multiple organizations are relying on similar systems to evaluate talent in similar ways. As talent acquisition professionals, we should ask an important question: Are we identifying the best candidates, or are we simply identifying the candidates who fit a predefined pattern? In my experience, the answer is often the latter. I've seen candidates successfully transition betwee n industries because their leadership skills were transferable. I've seen individuals with nontraditional backgrounds outperform candidates who appeared to be perfect matches on paper. Those opportunities only exist when someone is willing to look beyond the resume. Algorithms cannot have that co nversation. What Great Talent Acquisition Really Looks Like The most successful hiring strategies start with understanding people. Before we begin recruiting for a client, the BBSI team spends time learning about the business itself. We want to understand: The company's culture Leadership style Business goals Team dynamics Workforce challenges Long-term growth plans Only then can we identify candidates who are not just qualified, but positioned to succeed. Finding talent is not about filling an opening; i t's about helping organizations build stronger teams and helping individuals find opportunities where they can thrive. That requires experience, judgment, and partnership. Why Relationships Matter More Than Ever One of the biggest differences between automated hiring and effective talent acquisition is feedback. Technology can screen a candidate People can coach one At BBSI , we spend time preparing candidates for interviews, understanding their career goals, and helping them present their strengths effectively. We also work closely with hiring managers to refine requirements, adjust expectations, and provide market insights throughout the process. That ongoing dialogue creates better outcomes for everyone involved. C andidates feel supported, employers feel understood, and hiring decisions become more informed. No algorithm can replace that relationship. The Value of Local Talent Expertise Because l abor markets, industries, and workforce challenges vary, what works in one market may not work in another. That's why BBSI's Talent Acquisition Team combines recruiting expertise with local market knowledge . Our teams understand the communities they serve, the industries they support, and the workforce realities employers face every day. This allows us to deliver recommendations based on real-world insight rather than generalized assumptions. For employers, that means access to talent strategies that are practical, responsive, and aligned with business goals. Talent Acquisition Is More Than Recruiting Many business leaders think of recruiting as simply filling open positions. In reality, effective talent acquisition is a growth strategy. The right hiring decisions can improve productivity, strengthen culture, reduce turnover, and support long-term business performance. The wrong hiring decisions can create costly setbacks that impact teams for months or even years. That's why we approach talent acquisition as a partnership rather than a transaction. Whether a company engages BBSI for standalone Talent Acquisition solutions or leverages our recruiting expertise as part of a broader workforce management partnership, our objective remains the same: helping businesses build the teams they need to grow. The Future of Hiring Is Human-Led & Technology-Enabled The future of hiring is not about choosing between technology and people. The strongest organizations will leverage both. Technology can help us move faster. It can help us organize information, improve efficiency, and support decision-making. But people... Provide context, Provide judgement, Recognize potential, and build relationships. Those are the factors that continue to drive successful hiring outcomes. At BBSI, we believe technology should support the hiring process , not define it. Our Talent Acquisition Team combines proven recruiting expertise, local market knowledge, and a hands-on partnership approach to help businesses identify, attract, and retain exceptional talent. Because great hiring has never been about finding great resumes, it's about finding great people. About the Author Raouia Makhoul is BBSI’s Vice President of Talent Acquisition, bringing more than 20 years of experience in staffing, recruiting, and workforce solutions. She is recognized for delivering exceptional talent and service to organizations across a wide range of industries, with deep expertise in Technology, Accounting, Finance, Human Resources, and Marketing. In her role, she leads talent acquisition strategy, recruitment operations, client partnerships, and team development, helping businesses build high-performing workforces while driving growth and operational excellence. A relationship-focused leader, Raouia is passionate about connecting people and opportunities. Throughout her career, including executive leadership roles at STAFFOGEN and Robert Half , she has built a reputation for understanding the unique goals of clients and candidates and creating lasting, successful partnerships. She is also deeply committed to mentoring and developing recruiting professionals, fostering collaborative teams, and empowering individuals and organizations to reach their full potential.

title: Ryde Advances Regional Expansion Strategy with Entry into Hong Kong Mobility Market
body_text: SINGAPORE, SG / ACCESS Newswire / April 14, 2026 / Ryde Group Ltd (NYSE: RYDE ) ("Ryde" or the "Company"), a leading technology platform for mobility and quick commerce in Singapore, today announced its strategic expansion into the Hong Kong market. This milestone marks a significant step in Ryde's regional growth strategy and strengthens its position as a key player in Asia's evolving mobility landscape. Entry into Hong Kong with Scalable Mobility Infrastructure As part of this expansion, Ryde will acquire up to 50 Hong Kong taxi licenses and deploy up to 50 electric vehicles ("EVs"). This initial rollout is intended to establish a capital-efficient and scalable operating base in one of Asia's most densely populated and high-demand mobility markets. By integrating licensed taxi operations with EV deployment, Ryde will introduce a differentiated, technology-enabled service offering aimed at improving driver economics, enhancing rider experience and supporting the transition toward lower-emission urban transportation. Expanding Geographic Footprint to Drive Revenue Growth The Company's entry into Hong Kong represents a strategic step in diversifying its geographic exposure and unlocking new revenue opportunities beyond its home market of Singapore. Leveraging its proprietary platform, established driver network model and operational expertise, Ryde is well-positioned to scale efficiently while adapting to local regulatory and market conditions. This expansion is expected to strengthen network effects, increase platform utilization and support more resilient, multi-market revenue streams over time. Positioned to Capture Demand in a High-Value Urban Mobility Market "Expanding into Hong Kong marks an important milestone in Ryde's growth journey," said James Tan, Chief Product Officer of Ryde. "We are entering a market with strong and consistent demand for mobility services, and a clear shift toward more efficient and sustainable solutions. Our focus is to establish a reliable operating base first, before scaling with discipline. This positions us to deliver long-term value to our shareholders." Advancing a Scalable, Asset-Enabled Growth Strategy This expansion underscores Ryde's broader strategy of combining platform technology with targeted asset deployment to accelerate growth and strengthen its competitive positioning. By entering key gateway cities such as Hong Kong, the Company aims to build a scalable regional mobility ecosystem that delivers sustainable, long-term value for customers, drivers and investors. About Ryde Group Ltd Ryde is a super mobility app founded in Singapore and recognised as the world's FIRST on-demand carpooling app since 2014. As a publicly listed company on the NYSE American, Ryde is reimagining the way people and goods move around by offering a full suite of services, including carpooling, private hire, taxi, and delivery. What distinguishes Ryde is its commitment to empowering private-hire and taxi partners by taking 0% commission, ensuring that drivers retain more of their hard-earned earnings. title: How to Book a Hotel Room Block for Your Wedding (2026 Guide)
summary: A hotel room block reserves a set of rooms at a negotiated rate for your out-of-town guests. Getting this right saves guests money, keeps everyone close
body_text: Last Updated on July 10, 2026 by Joy Editors A hotel room block reserves a set of rooms at a negotiated rate for your out-of-town guests. Getting this right saves guests money, keeps everyone close together, and removes a major logistical headache from your planning list. Quick answer: Contact 2-3 hotels near your venue 9-12 months before the wedding. Request a courtesy or contracted block for 20-30% of your guest count. Negotiate the rate, set a guest booking deadline (4-6 weeks before the wedding), and share the booking link on your wedding website. What Is a Hotel Room Block? A hotel room block is a reserved group of rooms at a specific hotel, held at a negotiated rate for your wedding guests. The hotel sets aside those rooms until a cutoff date, after which any unbooked rooms return to general inventory. Room blocks serve two purposes: they guarantee your guests a place to stay at a lower rate, and they keep your wedding party and out-of-town guests in the same location, which makes transportation and post-wedding gatherings much easier to coordinate. Courtesy Block vs Contracted Block Type Financial Obligation Best For Courtesy block None: rooms released if unbooked Smaller weddings, uncertain guest count Contracted block Attrition clause (pay for % of unbooked rooms) Larger weddings, high out-of-town guest count Most couples with under 75 guests can negotiate a courtesy block. Larger weddings typically need a contracted block to secure enough rooms, but the attrition clause requires careful negotiation. Hotel Room Block Timeline Timing matters more than most couples expect. Here is a month-by-month timeline for booking and managing your hotel room block. When What to Do 12 months out Start researching hotels near your venue. Identify 2-3 options at different price points. 9-10 months out Contact hotel sales departments. Request group rates, availability, and contract terms. Compare offers. 8 months out Negotiate final terms and sign the contract. Confirm the cutoff date, attrition clause, and complimentary perks. 7 months out Add hotel block details and booking link to your wedding website . 6 months out Include hotel information on save-the-dates or a follow-up email. 3-4 months out Send wedding invitations with the hotel booking link and cutoff date prominently listed. 6-8 weeks before Send a booking reminder to all guests who have not reserved a room yet. 4-6 weeks before Cutoff date arrives. Unbooked rooms return to general inventory. Check final numbers with the hotel. 2 weeks before Confirm final room count, any complimentary upgrades, and early check-in or late checkout arrangements. Wedding week Share check-in details and parking info with guests. Confirm the hotel has your welcome bags (if applicable). Pro tip: If your wedding falls during peak season (May through October) or near a major holiday, start the hotel search 12-14 months out. Popular venues in destination wedding cities like Charleston, Napa, or Savannah can sell out an entire year in advance. How Much Does a Hotel Room Block Cost? The short answer: a courtesy block costs you nothing unless guests do not book. A contracted block can cost you money if rooms go unfilled. Here is what to expect in real numbers. Group Rate Discounts Hotels typically offer 10-25% off the standard nightly rate for a room block. The discount depends on the hotel, the number of rooms, the season, and how much leverage you have (more rooms = better rate). Hotel Type Standard Rate (per night) Typical Group Rate Savings per Room Budget/mid-range $120-180 $100-150 $20-30 Upscale (Marriott, Hilton) $200-300 $170-250 $30-50 Luxury/resort $350-600+ $280-500 $50-100+ Real Savings Examples These examples show what a room block can save your guests in total: Small wedding (15 rooms, 2 nights, mid-range hotel): Standard rate $160/night, group rate $130/night. Savings: $30 x 15 rooms x 2 nights = $900 total saved across all guests Medium wedding (25 rooms, 2 nights, upscale hotel): Standard rate $250/night, group rate $200/night. Savings: $50 x 25 rooms x 2 nights = $2,500 total saved Destination wedding (40 rooms, 3 nights, resort): Standard rate $400/night, group rate $320/night. Savings: $80 x 40 rooms x 3 nights = $9,600 total saved The Attrition Cost Risk If you sign a contracted block with an 80% attrition clause and block 25 rooms, you must fill at least 20 rooms. If only 15 rooms get booked, you could owe the hotel for 5 unbooked rooms at the group rate. Example: 5 unbooked rooms x $200/night x 2 nights = $2,000 out of pocket. This is why starting with a conservative block size is important. You can always add rooms, but you cannot easily remove them from a contract. Pro tip: Ask the hotel if they offer a “review date” 60-90 days before the wedding where you can adjust the block size up or down without penalty. Many hotels are willing to include this, especially for courtesy blocks. How Many Rooms to Reserve A common starting point is 30-40% of your total guest count. For a 150-person wedding, that is 20-25 rooms. For a 200-person wedding, plan for 30-35 rooms. Adjust based on: Out-of-town guests: If 60% of your guests are traveling, block more rooms Destination wedding: Nearly all guests need accommodations: block 70-80% of your count Local wedding: Block fewer rooms; many guests will drive home Multi-night events: Account for rehearsal dinner and post-wedding brunch nights Pro tip: Start conservative and ask the hotel about their policy for adding rooms later. Most hotels will add rooms to your block if demand is high, as long as inventory allows. Step-by-Step: How to Book a Hotel Room Block Step 1 Identify 2-3 Hotels Near Your Venue Look for hotels within 10-15 minutes of your ceremony and reception venue. Prioritize properties with a mix of room types (standard, suites) and price points so guests with different budgets can find something that works. Step 2 Contact the Sales or Events Department Call or email the hotel’s sales or group events department directly (not the front desk). Explain that you are planning a wedding, give the dates, and ask about group room block availability and rates. Most hotels have a dedicated wedding coordinator or group sales manager. Step 3 Negotiate the Rate and Terms Ask for a group rate that is 10-20% below the standard room rate. Also negotiate: Attrition percentage (aim for 80% or lower, or a courtesy block with no obligation) Cutoff date for guests to book (4-6 weeks before the wedding) Complimentary rooms (many hotels offer 1 free room per 10-20 booked) Complimentary suite upgrade for the couple Early check-in or late checkout for the wedding party Step 4 Review and Sign the Contract Read the attrition clause carefully. It specifies what percentage of rooms you must fill and what you owe if you fall short. A standard clause requires 80-90% fill. If you cannot negotiate it lower, consider a smaller initial block size. Step 5 Share the Booking Link with Guests Once the block is confirmed, add the booking information to your wedding website . Include the hotel name, address, group rate, booking code or link, and the cutoff date. Send a reminder 6-8 weeks before the cutoff. Questions to Ask the Hotel Before signing any contract, get clear answers to these questions. Print this list or save it on your phone for your first call with the hotel’s sales team. Rates and Availability What is the group rate per night, and how does it compare to the standard rate? Is the rate available for all room types (standard, king, suite)? Are there different rates for weeknights vs weekends? Can guests extend their stay at the group rate before or after the wedding dates? Is the rate locked, or can it change before the cutoff date? Contract and Attrition Is this a courtesy block or a contracted block? What is the attrition percentage? (Aim for 80% or lower.) What exactly do we owe if the block is not filled? Is there a review date where we can adjust the block size without penalty? What is the cutoff date for guest bookings? Can we add rooms to the block after signing if demand is higher than expected? Complimentary Perks Do you offer a complimentary room for the couple? (Common at 1 per 10-20 rooms booked.) Is a suite upgrade available for the wedding night? Can the wedding party get early check-in or late checkout? Is there a hospitality suite or common area available for the wedding party? Do you offer a welcome bag delivery service for guest rooms? Logistics What is the distance to the venue, and do you offer a shuttle service? What are the parking options and costs? Is there a group booking link or code for guests? What is the cancellation policy for individual guests within the block? Do you have accessible rooms available within the block? Pro tip: Ask about shuttle service even if the hotel does not advertise it. Many hotels will arrange a complimentary or discounted shuttle for groups of 20+ rooms. This eliminates the need for rideshare coordination on the wedding night. What to Say When Contacting Hotels Here is a sample email to send to a hotel’s sales department: Subject: Wedding Room Block Inquiry: [Your Names], [Wedding Date] Hello, We are getting married at [venue name] on [date] and are looking to reserve a hotel room block for our guests. We expect approximately [number] out-of-town guests and would like to reserve [number] rooms for [number] nights, from [check-in date] to [check-out date]. Could you please send information about your group rates, room availability, and contract terms? We are also interested in any complimentary amenities available for wedding groups. Thank you, [Your names] How to Add Hotel Block Info to Your Wedding Website Your wedding website’s travel and accommodations page is where guests will look for hotel information. Include: Hotel name and address Group rate per night Direct booking link or phone number with group code Booking deadline (emphasize this: guests miss it more than anything else) Distance from the venue Parking information Joy’s hotel room block tool lets couples search hotels, reserve a block, and generate a shareable booking link directly from their wedding website. Guests see the negotiated rate and book without needing a separate code or phone call. Pro tip: Send a reminder to guests 6 weeks before the booking cutoff. Include the direct booking link and the exact deadline. Many guests intend to book but forget. One reminder email cuts your attrition risk significantly. Wording for Your Wedding Invitation Details Card Keep it brief on the details card. Direct guests to your wedding website for the full booking instructions: A block of rooms has been reserved for our guests at [Hotel Name], [address]. Please book by [cutoff date] to receive the group rate. Visit [wedding website URL] for booking details. Common Hotel Room Block Mistakes Booking too late: Popular hotels near popular venues fill up fast. Start 9-12 months out. Overestimating the block size: A large block with a strict attrition clause can cost you money if guests do not fill it. Start smaller. Missing the cutoff date: The couple is responsible for communicating the deadline clearly. Send at least two reminders. Not reading the attrition clause: This is the most expensive mistake. Know exactly what you owe if the block is not filled. Forgetting to add the booking link to the website: Guests cannot book what they cannot find. Frequently Asked Questions How many hotel rooms should I block for my wedding? A common rule of thumb is to block rooms for 30-40% of your guest count. For a 150-person wedding, that means 20-25 rooms. Start with a conservative estimate: most hotels allow you to add rooms later if demand is high. When should I book a hotel room block for my wedding? Book your hotel room block 9-12 months before the wedding. Popular venues and peak season dates (May-October) require even more lead time. The block should be set up before you send save the dates so guests can book immediately. Do I have to pay for hotel rooms my guests do not book? It depends on the contract. Attrition clauses require you to pay for a percentage of unbooked rooms (typically 80-90% of the block). Courtesy blocks have no financial obligation but may have fewer rooms. Always clarify the attrition policy before signing. What is the difference between a courtesy block and a contracted block? A courtesy block holds rooms with no financial commitment but rooms are released if not booked by the cutoff date. A contracted block guarantees the rate and room availability but includes an attrition clause requiring you to pay for a minimum percentage of rooms. Joy’s built-in hotel room block tool lets you search hotels, reserve a block, and share a booking link with guests, all from your wedding website.

title: Streamex Corp. Announces 24/7, 365 Instant Liquidity for GLDY Through Collaboration with Wintermute
summary: Highlights Buying or selling GLDY is now instant. With Wintermute acting as a continuous liquidity provider, both purchases and redemptions of GLDY now complete in real time, T+0. What previously took two business days now happens immediately, around the clock, 365 days a year.
body_text: drafts Investor Sign-ups Streamex Corp. Announces 24/7, 365 Instant Liquidity for GLDY Through Collaboration with Wintermute July 23, 2026 PDF Version Streamex Corp. Announces 24/7, 365 Instant Liquidity for GLDY Through Collabora… Highlights Buying or selling GLDY is now instant. With Wintermute acting as a continuous liquidity provider, both purchases and redemptions of GLDY now complete in real time, T+0. What previously took two business days now happens immediately, around the clock, 365 days a year. GLDY now has approximately $12 million in secondary market liquidity across multiple avenues, available 24/7, 365. WINTER PARK, Fla., July 23, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Streamex Corp. (“Streamex” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: STEX), a technology company building the future of the commodity markets through tokenization, today announced that Wintermute, an independent third-party proprietary trading firm, has expanded liquidity for GLDY, the Company’s gold-backed, yield-bearing tokenized security. Under the arrangement, eligible GLDY holders can now access instant third-party liquidity through our interface. Streamex has seeded 1,069 GLDY and $5,000,000 USDC with Wintermute, bringing total secondary market liquidity to approximately $12 million USD across multiple venues. The addition of Wintermute as a liquidity provider is designed to improve the GLDY investor experience. Previously, both the purchase and redemption process for GLDY settled on a T+2 basis, a two-business-day clearing cycle consistent with traditional securities markets. Now, both processes settle instantly at T+0. An investor who decides to buy or sell GLDY today does not wait, the transaction clears immediately, in real time, within approximately 10 bps of the spot gold market price, supported by institutional infrastructure, subject to market conditions, applicable liquidity limits, and the functionality of third-party blockchain infrastructure. For all investors, Wintermute’s liquidity will be available directly through the Streamex platform, enabling purchases and redemptions to be executed natively within the Streamex application, streamlining the investor experience from discovery to settlement in a single interface. Combined with the Orca permissioned pool infrastructure, and tZero’s ATS, GLDY’s total secondary market liquidity now stands at approximately $12 million. Investors can access this liquidity on their own schedule, not during exchange hours, not subject to T+2 clearing, but continuously and immediately. Investor Questions: What You Need to Know Is there a limit on how much I can buy or sell at once? Individual orders through the Streamex interface are subject to a maximum of 1,000 GLDY tokens or $4.5 million USD per 48-hour period. Institutional investors seeking to transact above these thresholds may do so directly OTC with Wintermute. How long does it take? Instant. Both purchases and redemptions through Wintermute settle in real time at T+0. There is no waiting period. Does this cost anything extra? There is no added trading fee. As with any market, transactions are subject to a bid-ask spread, which varies based on order size and market conditions. No additional fees are charged beyond the spread. Is this available right now? Yes. Wintermute began quoting prices and bid/ask spreads for GLDY as of last week. The liquidity is live. Henry McPhie, Co-Founder & Chief Executive Officer of Streamex, said: “T+0 settlement is something traditional financial markets have spent years working toward for equities. GLDY has it today, for a tokenized gold security. What that means in practice is simple: investors are no longer waiting two days to have their transaction cleared. They buy, they own. They sell, they receive proceeds. That is how it should work, and that is now how GLDY works.” About Wintermute Wintermute is one of the world’s leading algorithmic trading and market-making firms, providing liquidity across major centralized exchanges, decentralized protocols, and OTC markets globally. title: Cosmic Rundown: Bento Slides, Passkey Frustrations, and Intel's High-NA EUV Milestone
summary: Daily developer news covering Bento's single-file presentations, passkey usability debates, Intel's High-NA EUV milestone, Postgres startup tips, and Elixir running in the browser.
body_text: Bento: Presentations as Single HTML Files A new project called Bento takes a minimalist approach to slide decks. The entire presentation lives in one HTML file that handles editing, viewing, data storage, and real-time collaboration. No cloud dependency, no proprietary format lock-in. For teams tired of wrestling with bloated presentation software or worrying about offline access, this is an interesting direction. The Hacker News discussion explores use cases ranging from internal documentation to conference talks. The Passkey Debate Continues A viral thread sparked by a tweet claiming passkeys were "invented by engineers with zero understanding of consumer brain" has reignited the authentication wars. The core tension: passkeys solve real security problems but introduce UX friction that confuses average users. Cross-device sync remains messy. Recovery flows are unclear. And the mental model of "something I have" doesn't translate well when that something lives invisibly in a password manager. For developers building authentication systems, this is a reminder that technical superiority doesn't guarantee adoption. The best security is security people actually use. Intel Ships High-NA EUV Silicon In chip manufacturing news, Intel announced they're shipping silicon produced with High-NA EUV lithography. This is a significant milestone in semiconductor manufacturing, pushing the boundaries of what's physically possible in chip production. For those outside the hardware world: EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography enables smaller, denser chip features. High-NA (numerical aperture) is the next evolution, allowing even finer patterns. This matters for everyone building software because it determines the performance ceiling of the hardware your code runs on. Postgres Survival Guide for Startups A practical guide from Hatchet covers the common Postgres pitfalls that catch startups off guard. Topics include connection pooling, index maintenance, query optimization, and knowing when to scale. If you're running Postgres in production, the full discussion includes battle-tested advice from engineers who've learned these lessons the hard way. Elixir in the Browser with Hologram Hologram now runs Elixir directly in the browser. This compiles Elixir to WebAssembly, enabling full-stack Elixir applications without a JavaScript frontend. For teams already invested in the Elixir ecosystem, this could simplify architecture significantly. The project page details the technical approach and current limitations. Quick Hits Formal verification with Lean : A beginner-friendly tutorial introduces mathematical proof verification. Useful for anyone curious about provably correct software. Apollo 11 source code : The original guidance computer code for the lunar modules is on GitHub. A fascinating look at mission-critical software from 1969. AI data center opposition : According to Redfin, most Americans don't want AI data centers in their neighborhoods. Infrastructure buildout meets NIMBY resistance. title: Top 8 Onboarding Software for Small Business in 2025
summary: Streamline new hire onboarding with top software solutions like Rippling, BambooHR, and Paylocity.
body_text: Bringing on new hires is an exciting step for any business. But the onboarding process can be overwhelming, especially for small teams. There’s paperwork to complete, accounts to set up, and training to organize. And you've got to do it all while making sure new employees feel supported from day one. Without a structured onboarding system, things can slip through the cracks easily. This can lead to confusion, delays, and a rocky start for the new hire. That’s where onboarding software comes in. It simplifies the process by automating onboarding tasks and keeping everything in one place. Essentially, onboarding software can make it easier for both HR teams and employees to stay on track. In this guide, we explain exactly what onboarding software is, how it works, and why small businesses can benefit from using it. We cover some of the top onboarding platform options available in 2025, key features to look for, and how to choose the right solution for your company. What is onboarding software? Onboarding software is a digital tool that helps businesses manage bringing in new employees. Instead of handling everything manually, like sending documents, tracking progress, and setting up accounts, companies use onboarding systems to organize and automate things. These platforms create a structured onboarding process, guiding both HR teams and new hires through each step. They typically include features like the distribution of digital paperwork, e-signatures, task tracking, and automated reminders. Many modern systems also integrate with payroll, benefits, and other HR tools. This can help businesses set up everything correctly for the new employee from the very start. Why do small businesses need onboarding software tools? Bringing on a new hire goes beyond just filling a vacant position. It involves setting the new hire up for success from the get-go. Small businesses generally work with limited time and resources, and a disorganized onboarding process only makes things harder. Without the right system in place, mistakes can pile up, HR wastes time, and new hires struggle to get up to speed. Here’s why small businesses need onboarding software to keep things running smoothly: Every hire counts Small businesses typically run on tight schedules. So, every new hire needs to hit the ground running. A disconnected onboarding process can make things take longer than they need to. It can leave HR buried in paperwork and new employees struggling to find their footing. Without a structured onboarding system, tasks can get missed, communication may break down, and productivity can become far from optimal. First impressions matter Employee onboarding involves more than paperwork. It’s the first real experience someone has with a company. A strong onboarding process sets the tone for new employees and helps them feel welcome. When businesses get onboarding right, employees are likely to feel more confident, engaged, and ready to stay long term. Mistakes cost time and money Small teams can’t afford onboarding mistakes. Not getting a payroll setup right, skipping compliance steps, or delaying employee training can create frustration for both HR and new hires. Then there's the fixing of these issues, which wastes time and can slow down operations. A structured onboarding process prevents these problems before they happen. Employees expect a good experience People typically want more than just a job. They want to feel valued. A smooth employee onboarding process helps them feel like part of the team from day one. When businesses invest in better onboarding, they can keep employees happy, motivated, and more likely to stay. 5 Benefits of onboarding software platform for small business By replacing manual processes with automation, onboarding software can help companies save time, reduce errors, and give their new hires a smoother start. Below are some of the major benefits of using onboarding software in a small business: 1. Efficiency Manual onboarding eats up valuable time. HR teams juggle emails, forms, and reminders, which often leads to confusion and delays. Manually following an onboarding checklist makes it easy to miss steps and slows everything down. An onboarding platform fixes this by centralizing tasks, automating paperwork, and keeping everything in one place. Instead of chasing signatures or tracking tasks manually, businesses can let the software handle it. What might take hours without onboarding software can take just minutes with it. Example: A small marketing agency hires a new graphic designer. Without onboarding software, HR spends hours emailing forms, collecting signatures, and setting up software accounts one by one. With an onboarding platform, the designer receives a single link that walks them through signing documents, setting up their email, and accessing design tools. And it does it all in under 30 minutes. 2. Compliance Small businesses can’t afford compliance mistakes. Missing key documents, skipping legal requirements, or mishandling tax forms can lead to penalties. Onboarding software can help keep everything in check by automating compliance steps, ensuring the right forms get signed, and securely storing records for audits. Example: A local café hires a new barista. The café needs to collect an I-9 form for work eligibility and tax withholding documents for payroll from the new barista. Without an onboarding system, the manager collects these by hand and may forget key forms. With onboarding software, the barista receives automatic prompts to upload their documents before their first shift, helping the café comply with labor laws. 3. Better employee experience A clunky onboarding process can make new hires feel lost before they even get started. An onboarding platform can do a good job of simplifying the experience. It can make it easy for them to access documents, complete training, and get introduced to the team. A smooth start can help new hires feel confident, engaged, and connected with the company culture from their very first day. Example: A tech startup hires a remote developer. Without onboarding software, the developer has to email HR for information and wait days to get access to necessary tools. With an onboarding platform, they log in on day one, complete their paperwork online, watch a welcome video from leadership, and instantly access Slack and Jira. This helps them feel like part of the team right away. 4. Automate HR processes Without automation, HR teams may spend hours on repetitive tasks. For instance, sending welcome emails, collecting forms, and setting up accounts. Onboarding software takes care of these steps automatically. This can free up HR to focus on bigger priorities like employee engagement and business growth. Example: A boutique law firm hires a legal assistant. Without an onboarding platform, HR manually sends IT setup instructions, tracks down signed NDAs, and adds the assistant to the payroll system. With automation, the assistant follows step-by-step instructions, signs all necessary documents electronically, and completes payroll enrollment, all without HR lifting a finger. 5. Streamline new employee training Onboarding doesn’t stop at the initial paperwork. New hires often need training to do their jobs well. With the right onboarding platform, businesses can seamlessly schedule training sessions, track progress, and make sure employees get the information they need to succeed. Instead of relying on scattered emails and informal check-ins, companies can deliver a structured training experience that sets employees up for success from the start. Example: A family-owned construction company hires a site supervisor. The role requires OSHA safety training, but without onboarding software, training happens through printed manuals and in-person meetings, leading to inconsistent learning. With an onboarding platform, the supervisor watches interactive safety modules, completes quizzes, and receives certification before stepping on site. Compliantly hire, onboard, and pay global employees. See Rippling The 8 best onboarding software for small business Choosing the right onboarding software is important for small businesses looking to streamline processes, stay compliant, and provide a smooth experience for new hires. Below, you can find a comparison of eight popular onboarding platforms , highlighting their key features, strengths, weaknesses, and potential use cases: 1. Rippling Rippling is an all-in-one workforce management platform and HR software that automates employee onboarding, payroll, IT provisioning, and compliance. Key features 90-second onboarding: Businesses can send offer letters, collect tax forms, enroll employees in payroll, and set up their software and device access fast. Automated compliance tracking: Rippling makes sure new hires complete I-9s, W-4s, and other mandatory documents, reducing compliance risks. Seamless IT setup: The system automatically creates accounts, assigns permissions, and provisions devices, eliminating manual IT work. Global onboarding capabilities: Companies can hire and pay employees or contractors worldwide without needing separate payroll or compliance solutions. Integrated benefits administration: Employees can enroll in health insurance, retirement plans, and other benefits during the onboarding process without HR manually managing it. Custom workflows and approvals: Businesses can tailor onboarding checklists and automate role-specific training, document sign-offs, and account setups. 30-, 60-, and 90-day check-ins: HR teams can set up automated reminders for performance reviews, surveys, and training milestones. Centralized employee data: Rippling syncs all employee information across HR, payroll, IT, and finance, eliminating duplicate data entry and reducing administrative work. Strengths Unlike many other onboarding platforms, Rippling connects hiring with payroll, benefits, and device setup in a single workflow. Small businesses can easily onboard and pay employees across multiple countries without third-party payroll providers. From sending offer letters to activating software accounts, Rippling eliminates manual tasks and streamlines the onboarding process. Rippling automatically tracks and stores required documents, helping companies meet legal requirements. Weaknesses A reliable internet access is necessary to use Rippling’s cloud-based platform for onboarding tasks. Small businesses must commit to a paid plan, as Rippling doesn't offer a free-tier option. Use cases Tech startups and remote-first companies: Businesses hiring remote employees benefit from Rippling’s automated IT provisioning and onboarding platform integrations. Small to mid-sized businesses scaling quickly : Companies that need a scalable onboarding solution can use Rippling to streamline hiring and compliance as they grow. Businesses hiring internationally: Rippling simplifies global employee onboarding by integrating international payroll, tax compliance, and local benefits. Companies managing multiple tools: Businesses that use Slack, Google Workspace, Zoom, and other apps can onboard employees without manually creating accounts. 2. Gusto Gusto is a payroll and HR platform that includes basic onboarding features for small businesses. Key features Basic digital onboarding: HR can send offer letters and collect e-signed documents. Payroll-integrated onboarding: New hires can input direct deposit details and tax forms within the onboarding flow. Built-in benefits enrollment : Employees can sign up for health insurance and retirement plans while completing their onboarding checklist. New hire state reporting: Gusto submits necessary paperwork for new employees to the appropriate state agencies. Limited integrations: The system connects with some third-party HR tools, but lacks the broad integration capabilities of more advanced onboarding platforms. Employee self-service portal: New hires can update their personal information and view payroll details. Strengths Gusto integrates payroll setup into new hire onboarding, which may make things easier for businesses focused primarily on payroll processing. Some users mention the platform has a beginner-friendly design. The flip side of this is that it lacks advanced customization or automation features, though. Weaknesses Gusto provides preset workflows with minimal flexibility, making it difficult for businesses to tailor onboarding processes, adjust automation, or modify the platform to fit unique company needs. Gusto's Employer of Record (EOR) service currently supports full-time employees only in Canada and India, which may not meet the needs of companies hiring in other countries. While the platform allows businesses to organize some onboarding tasks, it doesn’t automate the entire process beyond payroll and benefits enrollment. Use cases Small businesses with simple HR needs: Companies that only require basic employee onboarding for payroll and benefits may find Gusto sufficient. Businesses hiring mostly in the US: As Gusto doesn't largely support international payroll or compliance for employees, it may be a potential fit for domestic hiring. 3. Bamboo HR BambooHR is an HR software platform that includes onboarding features, with a focus on basic HR tasks, such as document collection, task tracking, and integrations. Key features Basic employee self-service onboarding: New hires can log in to complete forms, upload documents, and access necessary company information. E-signatures and document storage: HR can send offer letters and collect e-signed documents. Preboarding features: The platform enables businesses to engage new hires before their first day, though with limited customization. New hire welcome templates: BambooHR provides preset email templates for welcoming employees. Limited integration with third-party tools: The platform connects with some HR and payroll software. Basic task tracking: HR can assign tasks to new employees and managers. Strengths The platform provides a simple onboarding process without unnecessary complexity. BambooHR supports digital signatures for new hire documents. Weaknesses BambooHR doesn't provide full workflow automation for complex onboarding processes like IT provisioning or role-based task assignments. Businesses must still manage and track some steps manually. Some tasks, like training sessions and team introductions, require in-person meetings or virtual calls instead of being fully automated within the platform. Response times can vary, and users may experience delays when needing assistance with onboarding issues. Use cases Small businesses with basic HR needs: Companies that need simple onboarding tools for collecting documents, assigning tasks, and managing HR basics without advanced automation may consider BambooHR. Companies with in-office teams: Businesses that rely on in-person onboarding rather than fully remote, automated processes may find BambooHR sufficient for their needs. 4. Paylocity Paylocity is a payroll and HR platform that includes basic onboarding features for managing employee documents and compliance. Key features Digital onboarding documents: New hires can complete tax forms, direct deposit setup, and company policies electronically. Employee self-service portal: New employees can log in to update personal details and access company documents. Task tracking for HR: The system allows HR teams to assign and monitor onboarding tasks. Integrated payroll setup: New hires can enter payroll details during onboarding. Preboarding capabilities : Businesses can send onboarding documents before an employee's first day. HR compliance tracking: The system helps ensure new hires complete the necessary onboarding compliance checklists. Strengths Paylocity connects new hire onboarding directly to its payroll system. New hires can access their own onboarding checklist, update personal information, and submit tax documents without requiring constant HR intervention. Weaknesses Paylocity relies on third-party partners for certain features, which can lead to a fragmented user experience and potential inconsistencies across different functions. While Paylocity has expanded through Blue Marble, its system remains largely aimed at US-based businesses, limiting its ability to handle global compliance and international workforce needs. Large-scale businesses that require more customization and advanced workforce management tools can find Paylocity limiting. Use cases Businesses with a focus on payroll: Businesses that prioritize payroll accuracy and tax compliance over IT automation may find Paylocity suitable. the necessary Companies that require digital onboarding documents and task tracking but don't need extensive workflow automation may consider Paylocity. 5. Paycor Paycor is an HR and payroll software platform that includes onboarding tools with a focus on document management, compliance tracking, and task assignments. Key features Digital document collection: New hires can complete and e-sign forms, including tax documents and company policies. Automated onboarding checklists: HR teams can assign tasks, set deadlines, and track onboarding progress within the platform. Preboarding capabilities: Employers can send welcome emails and necessary paperwork before an employee's first day. Self-service portal: Employees can access their onboarding materials, update personal information, and complete assigned tasks without HR intervention. Basic compliance tracking: The system helps businesses ensure employees complete necessary onboarding steps for compliance. Limited integrations: Paycor connects with some payroll and HR tools. Strengths HR teams can assign role-specific tasks, monitor progress, and send reminders to ensure new hires complete the necessary steps. New hires can access forms, company documents, and training materials at their own pace without relying on HR for manual updates. Weaknesses Users report having to reload the application due to system crashes, which can slow down the onboarding process. Some users find contract setup and adjustments to be less intuitive than expected. The platform lacks flexibility for businesses that need to tailor onboarding workflows, forms, and automation to their specific processes. Use cases Small to mid-sized businesses: Companies that need a simple, structured onboarding process with basic task tracking and compliance support may consider Paycor. Businesses focused on payroll and HR: Organizations looking for a combined payroll and onboarding system rather than a fully automated IT and onboarding solution might find Paycor sufficient. 6. Deel Deel is a global payroll and compliance platform that offers onboarding tools for businesses hiring international employees and contractors. Key features Contract generation: Employers can create and send legally compliant contracts for different worker classifications. Document management: The platform allows businesses to collect and store important onboarding documents, including tax forms and IDs. Automated compliance tracking: Deel helps businesses adhere to international hiring laws by tracking local labor regulations. Payment processing: The system facilitates payroll for employees and contractors across multiple countries. Employee self-service onboarding: New hires can upload documents, review contracts, and complete necessary forms through a digital portal. Customizable onboarding workflows: Businesses can configure steps for new hires, such as preboarding document collection, contract sign-offs, and role-based compliance requirements. Strengths Deel provides hiring support for businesses navigating international labor laws. The platform allows companies to pay employees and contractors in multiple currencies without relying on external payroll providers. Weaknesses Deel focuses on compliance and payments rather than providing a structured onboarding experience with training, task tracking, or IT setup. Deel offethe necessaryfits packages may find Deel’s options restrictive, requiring additional effort to set up benefits beyond the platform's predefined offerings. Use cases Companies hiring international employees and contractors: Deel can be a suitable option for businesses that need to onboard and pay a globally distributed workforce. Organizations focused on compliance: Businesses that prioritize adherence to international labor laws over a fully automated onboarding workflow may consider Deel. 7. ADP ADP is a payroll and human capital management ( HCM ) platform that includes onboarding tools for businesses looking to streamline administrative processes. Key features Digital document management: New hires can complete and submit essential forms, such as tax withholding and direct deposit information, electronically. Manager task assignment and tracking: HR teams can assign and monitor onboarding tasks to managers. Mobile accessibility: New employees can complete necessary paperwork from any device. Introduction to company culture: The system includes features to share organizational values and culture through welcome videos and company information. Onboarding buddy system: New hires can connect with existing team members before their first day to ease the transition. Preboarding capabilities: New employees can complete onboarding tasks before their official start date to speed up the process. Strengths The onboarding system connects with ADP’s broader suite of HR and payroll tools, keeping all employee data in one platform. The system includes standardized workflows that align with common regulatory requirements. Weaknesses Some users report that the UI feels cluttered and difficult to navigate, leading to confusion during onboarding. The onboarding process requires users to go through multiple screens, which can feel excessive. The platform offers prebuilt templates but lacks flexibility for unique processes. Use cases Companies already using ADP for payroll and HR: Businesses that rely on ADP’s broader suite of HR and payroll tools may consider the onboarding system to keep all employee data within one platform. Businesses with standardized onboarding processes: Organizations that prefer prebuilt compliance workflows and structured templates over extensive customization may find ADP a potential option. 8. Paychex Paychex is a payroll and HR platform that includes basic onboarding tools for businesses looking to manage employee documentation and payroll setup in one system. Key features Electronic document management: New hires can complete and e-sign tax forms, direct deposit details, and other necessary paperwork digitally. Task automation: HR teams can assign tasks, set deadlines, and track completion within the platform. Preboarding capabilities: Employers can send offer letters, benefits information, and onboarding materials before an employee's first day. Employee self-service portal: New hires can access and update their information without needing HR involvement. Payroll integration: The system links new hire data directly with Paychex payroll processing. Third-party integrations: The platform connects with some external HR and payroll tools. Strengths Paychex provides a step-by-step process that helps standardize onboarding tasks for HR teams. The platform provides some built-in compliance tools to help businesses manage tax forms and employee documentation. Weaknesses The platform feels dated, with some users describing the interface as resembling software from decades ago. Many features don't have a dedicated menu button, requiring access strictly through notification cards on the dashboard homepage, which can be confusing. Finding the right support agent for a specific issue can be difficult, leading to delays in resolving problems. Use cases Businesses already using Paychex payroll: Companies that rely on Paychex for payroll processing may consider the onboarding system to keep all employee data within one platform. Small businesses with minimal onboarding needs: Organizations that require basic document collection and payroll setup without advanced automation or customization may find Paychex a potential option. Schedule a demo with Rippling today See Rippling How to choose the best small business onboarding software Not all onboarding platforms work the same way, and the wrong choice can cause more problems than it solves. Small businesses need a solution that fits their size, budget, and workflow. Here’s how to pick the best onboarding software for your company: Step 1. Evaluate your business needs and goals Start with the basics. What’s slowing down your onboarding process right now? Are new hires getting lost in paperwork? Is HR spending too much time on manual tasks? Do employees struggle with training because there’s no structured system? Make a list of the biggest pain points. If compliance is an issue, you’ll probably need a platform that automates document collection and tracks deadlines. If remote hiring is part of your business, look for software with digital signatures and virtual training tools. The goal is to find an onboarding system that fixes your specific problems, not just one with fancy features you won’t use. Step 2. Consider your present (and future) budget Price matters, but so does value. Some onboarding platforms charge per employee, while others have a flat monthly fee. Some include payroll and benefits, while others charge extra for those features. Think about what you can afford now, but also plan for the future. If your business is growing, you don’t want to switch software in a year because your current plan becomes too expensive. Compare different pricing models and check if the platform offers a scalable option. It's important that it grows with you. Step 3. Compare software integrations with current tools Your onboarding system should work with the tools you already use. If your payroll software, HR platform, or applicant tracking system (ATS) doesn’t sync with the new software, onboarding could remain a manual nightmare. Make a list of must-have integrations. If you already have a payroll system in place, ensure the onboarding platform connects seamlessly. If your team relies on a specific communication tool, check if the system can add new hires to the right channels straight away. The fewer manual steps, the better. Step 4. Check user reviews and customer support quality A platform can look great on paper but be a headache in real life. Read real user reviews, especially from businesses your size, to see if it actually delivers on its promises. Look for feedback on things like ease of use, setup time, and customer support responsiveness. Some platforms offer 24/7 chat, while others take days to reply. Try asking a pre-sales question and see how fast they respond. If getting help is already a hassle before you sign up, it probably won’t get any better later. 7 Essential features of onboarding systems for small businesses The right features can save time, reduce errors, and help new hires feel prepared from day one. Here are some of the must-have features to look for when choosing an onboarding platform for a small business: 1. Electronic documents and forms management Every new hire needs to complete paperwork. For example, tax forms, contracts, and NDAs. Handling these manually wastes time and increases the risk of errors. A good onboarding system lets employees fill out, sign, and submit documents electronically. Why it matters: Without digital document management, HR has to chase signatures, scan forms, and file paperwork manually. This slows down onboarding and creates room for lost documents and compliance risks. With an automated system, new hires complete everything online before their first day, keeping everything organized and secure. 2. Compliance Small businesses can’t afford compliance mistakes. Whether it’s tax forms, work eligibility verification, or industry-specific regulations, missing a step can lead to fines or legal trouble. A strong onboarding platform automates compliance tracking. It helps ensure that employees complete every necessary document on time. Why it matters: Manual compliance tracking often leads to missing or outdated paperwork. A proper onboarding system not only collects and stores compliance documents but also alerts HR when something needs attention. 3. Integration options Onboarding doesn’t happen in isolation. A good onboarding system should connect effortlessly with payroll, HR software, applicant tracking systems (ATS), and communication tools. This prevents duplicate data entry and facilitates smooth transitions for new hires. Why it matters: Without integrations, HR has to manually enter the same information across multiple platforms. This wastes time and increases the chances of mistakes. 4. Customizability Every business has a different onboarding process. A great onboarding platform lets companies customize workflows, forms, training schedules, and welcome messages to match their unique needs. It should adapt to different roles within the company, ensuring that executives, remote employees, and frontline staff all receive relevant onboarding experiences. Why it matters: A one-size-fits-all approach doesn’t work. The onboarding experience should reflect company policies, branding, and industry requirements. Without customization, businesses risk delivering a generic process that leaves new hires feeling disconnected or unprepared for their specific roles. 5. Scalability What works for a five-person company may not work when the team grows to 50. The right onboarding platform should support business growth, allowing for more employees, locations, and processes with no need for an overhaul. Why it matters: Switching systems every time the business expands is costly and disruptive. Choosing scalable software prevents future headaches. 6. User-friendly If HR and new hires struggle to use the software, it defeats the purpose. A great onboarding system should have a clean, intuitive interface that makes it easy to complete tasks without unnecessary complexity. Why it matters: Complicated software leads to frustration, delays, and incomplete onboarding steps. Employees should be able to navigate the system without constant IT support. 7. body_text: View All News W. R. Berkley Corporation Announces Senior Executive Appointments July 27, 2026 Download (opens in new window) Daniel R. Westcott Named Executive Vice President Robert R. Coyne, Jr. Appointed President of Berkley Re America GREENWICH, Conn.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- W. R. Berkley Corporation (NYSE: WRB) today announced the appointment of Daniel R. Westcott as executive vice president. Robert R. Coyne, Jr. will succeed Mr. Westcott as president of Berkley Re America. In addition, Robert C. Hewitt, executive vice president of the Company, has been named chairman of Berkley Re. The appointments are effective immediately. Mr. Westcott has nearly 30 years of experience in the property casualty reinsurance market. He joined Berkley Re America as president in 2019. Mr. Coyne joined Berkley in 2006 and became senior vice president of Berkley Re America in 2010. He has over 30 years of experience in the property casualty reinsurance business. Mr. Hewitt joined Berkley in 2002 as senior vice president for risk management and was named executive vice president of the Company in 2016. Commenting on the appointments, W. Robert Berkley, Jr., chairman, chief executive officer, and president of W. R. Berkley Corporation, said: "Rob, Dan, and Rob have all provided outstanding leadership within Berkley for many years. Dan’s skills and broad experience in the reinsurance market, as well as his extensive knowledge of our organization, will serve us well as he takes on oversight of our assumed reinsurance businesses. With deep expertise in developing reinsurance solutions for customers, Rob Coyne is very well-positioned to lead Berkley Re America forward to build upon its success. Rob Hewitt has made extraordinary contributions to Berkley during his tenure, and we are deeply appreciative of his leadership, judgment, and unwavering commitment to the Company. He has been a trusted colleague and valued leader, and we are especially pleased, both personally and professionally, that we will continue to benefit from his extensive experience and expertise.” Berkley Re is a global reinsurance leader, delivering exceptional underwriting and service to clients worldwide. It comprises Berkley Re America, Berkley Re UK, Berkley Re Solutions, Berkley Re Australia, and Berkley Re Asia. Berkley Re America provides specialized property and casualty reinsurance solutions throughout North America. For further information about the products and services available from Berkley Re, please visit www.berkleyre.com . Founded in 1967, W. R. Berkley Corporation is an insurance holding company that is among the largest commercial lines writers in the United States and operates worldwide in two segments of the property casualty insurance business: Insurance and Reinsurance & Monoline Excess. For further information about W. R. Berkley Corporation, please visit www.berkley.com . Karen A. Horvath Vice President – External Financial Communications 203-629-3000 Source: W. R.
